articles.title: Body found in Colombia in search for missing Anton Green
articles.summary: Anton Green's family are told a body found in Colombia is believed to be the missing 43-year-old.
articles.body:
The family of a British man missing in Colombia have been told a body has been found in the search for him.

Anton Green from Manchester had been living in the South American country for two-and-a-half years, but stopped responding to messages in August.

Earlier, his family in Whalley Range were told that a body had been discovered, and that it was believed to be the 43-year-old.

They told the BBC that the news - which came just hours after they had renewed their appeal for help finding him - had devastated them and that they were "trying to come to terms with what's happened".

A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) spokesman confirmed that the body of a British man had been found in Colombia.

Anton's family had told the BBC that his failure to contact his family had been out of character.

His mother, Nylva McKie-Williams, had said his last words to her in August were "we will speak at the weekend".

She told BBC North West Tonight he had kept in frequent touch with his family, and that it had been "so unlike him not to be in contact with us".

Last month, footballer Marcus Rashhford got behind the appeal to find him, describing him as a "family friend".

Anton's brother Ro-Shaun Williams had been part of the Manchester United youth team alongside Rashford.

Anton's sister Sian Tuohey described her brother as a "happy, decent guy" who had been living in Colombia for three years, having settled there while travelling.

He spoke fluent Spanish and, not long before contact was lost, had moved to the Fontibon area of the capital, Bogota.

The news of the discovery of a body was broken to the family by police in the early hours of Thursday, the BBC understands.

His relatives said they were now waiting on more information from the Attorney General's Office in Bogota.

An FCDO spokesman said: "We are aware of the death of a British national in Colombia and are providing support to their family."

articles.title: Meet Franz Lozano Jr., the Texas student who returned to education after more than a decade away; he is now part of a national award-winning student organisation recognised for leadership, service and community engagement
articles.summary: Returning to college after more than a decade away can be daunting enough.
articles.body: Returning to college after more than a decade away can be daunting enough. For Franz Lozano Jr., it became the beginning of an unexpected leadership journey. A biomedical equipment technology student at San Jacinto College, Lozano returned to education after serving in the U.S. Army and working in industrial fields. He eventually reconnected with learning while also helping shape conversations around education and the people who make it possible. According to a news report by the San Jacinto College, Lozano's path into advocacy began almost by accident. Encouraged by a friend, Lozano joined the Texas State Teachers Association of Aspiring Educators, despite not studying to become a teacher. What started as an extracurricular commitment soon became a space where he could develop his leadership skills, meet fellow students and find new ways to serve his community. Scroll down to read his interesting journey.From local projects to national recognitionThe San Jacinto College chapter has now earned national attention, receiving the National Outstanding Community College Chapter Award at the National Education Association Aspiring Educators Conference in Denver, states the news report.The award recognises student organisations that demonstrate leadership, service, professional development and meaningful community engagement. Five San Jacinto students, including Lozano, represented the chapter at the conference alongside Alexis Gonzalez, Lilly Maldonado, Alexandra Martinez and Jordan Potter, adds the report.The recognition reflects work that begins much closer to home. Students have participated in initiatives designed to make a tangible difference in their communities, including the Kindness Project, which involved creating messages of encouragement for cancer patients, senior citizens and children in hospitals and care facilities.They also developed grant-writing skills and secured funding to establish a garden club at a local elementary school, turning classroom learning into community action.Finding a voice through serviceFor Lozano, the organisation has become more than a student activity. His involvement has helped him understand the connection between education, public policy and government, eventually leading him towards advocacy for students and future educators, explains the report. He has since risen to become president of the Central Campus chapter and state vice president of the Texas State Teachers Association of Aspiring Educators.His choice of biomedical equipment technology also reflects a practical desire to combine technical skills with service. The programme offered hands-on learning while allowing him to work in a field that ultimately helps people. His involvement with TSTA-AE gave that instinct for service another dimension.Learning beyond the classroomThe national conference offered students an opportunity to exchange ideas with aspiring educators from across the country while attending workshops focused on recruitment, advocacy and issues affecting students and educators. For some, the trip also represented a rare chance to travel beyond familiar surroundings and experience a national professional community firsthand.That momentum continued after the conference with San Jacinto College's first TSTA-AE Leadership Retreat, held on August 29 at the Central Campus. The programme focused on strengthening leadership, communication and relationship-building skills.As per the online report, Lozano's journey illustrates how returning to education can lead somewhere entirely unexpected. What began as a second chapter in his own academic life has evolved into an opportunity to help others find their voices, serve their communities and see how even small acts of leadership can contribute to something much larger.Images Courtesy: istock and San Jacinto CollegeYou use AI every day. articles.title: In 1951 Kobe, the centuries-old Japanese 'uchimizu' ritual was used to cool hot pavement; later experiments found it could also cool the surrounding air
articles.summary: Explore the age-old Japanese ritual of Uchimizu that provides natural cooling during summer heat. Discover its effectiveness, significance, and modern revival in urban settings.
articles.body: An ancient custom still appears in front of stores and homes during the warmest weeks of the Japanese summer. A ladle is picked up, a bucket is filled, and water is thrown across the parched land. The idea behind the technique, known as uchimizu, is that the water will lessen the heat's pain. As cities get hotter, researchers have become increasingly curious about it. Organisers of Mission Uchimizu, a Japanese effort that began in 2003, put it plainly: water has a high heat of vaporisation, so when it evaporates after being sprinkled, it draws heat out of the ground. The program began as a social experiment to see if summer temperatures could be reduced by two degrees Celsius if one million individuals sprayed water at the same time.One image in particular captures how firmly rooted the habit was in everyday life: a 1951 photograph from Kobe showing a woman splashing water across a roadway. The photographer was an amateur named Koji Takashima, and the woman in the frame was reportedly his wife, though the attribution hasn't been independently confirmed. The photograph is also said to have placed fifth in the black-and-white category of a Popular Photography magazine contest that year. Nobody was measuring temperatures with sensors back then; people simply knew the street felt better afterward, and it's only in recent years that scientists have checked whether that sense was right.How does the water coolEvaporation demands energy, and the water draws that energy from whatever it contacts, which in this case is the scorching pavement and the air directly above it. In a 2018 study published in the journal Water, researchers at Delft University of Technology identified two benefits: less radiant heat reaches your body because of the cooler surface, and the evaporating water also draws heat from the air itself.The same study traces the tradition back to the 17th century, noting it has been losing ground for the past 50 years or so. Air conditioning filled the void, and some people came to see older methods as too much work or unfashionable. Today, Japanese cities are attempting to revive uchimizu, including Tokyo, where municipal programmes have sponsored public events in recent years.What the Delft team measuredOn 24 August 2016, six uchimizu experiments were carried out on a brick paved street at their campus. They sprayed water over a three-metre square patch, then tracked the air above it with a one-metre cube of fibre-optic cables that measured temperature at more than 34,000 locations. These are some of the clearest figures to date on how Uchimizu actually performs.The air at a height of two metres was cooled by around 1.5 degrees Celsius. In a test run in the shadow of a tree, where the bricks started at 36 degrees and only a millimetre of water was utilised, the decrease was much greater closer to the ground, reaching 8.3 degrees at its highest.One or two millimetres made little difference, but soaking the bricks with more than five millimetres roughly doubled the cooling near the ground compared with one millimetre. The weakest result came on bricks that began at 47.7 degrees: the surface cooled to about 38 degrees, yet the air just above the ground barely cooled at all, a gap the researchers attribute to how quickly such hot bricks evaporated the water before it could draw much heat from the surrounding air.Testing it in publicJapanese municipal authorities have been testing the idea in public. The 2003 program was stated to have data at four Tokyo sites showing a lowering of around one degree Celsius on average. Most recently, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government sponsored uchimizu events in Ueno Park in the 2016 financial year and in Hibiya Midtown in 2018, according to NIES, Japan’s National Institute for Environmental Studies. Staff assessed the air temperature, humidity and radiant heat, then compared the readings with areas where nothing had been done.The Delft findings suggest several common-sense routines. The best results came on shaded pavement, and the test on very hot bricks showed almost no cooling of the air. The cooling effect lasts only as long as the pavement stays wet. In the Delft trial, it held for more than an hour, and while the added humidity was negligible in the Netherlands' climate: the researchers note it may be worth more consideration in damp regions.Tradition isn't only an old habit. The lesson is that a bucket of water on shaded pavement can cool the neighbouring air by a degree or more, though results vary with conditions, and it's a temporary effect that only works as long as the ground stays wet. The experts said the impacts on the city as a whole still need proper study, as does the question of how much water would be needed. But for an entrance or a courtyard, the woman in that 1951 photo had it right.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Syria calls for independent probe into sinking of ship in Black Sea
articles.summary: Syrian authorities questioned why search and rescue operations were called off before the fate of 10 sailors was known.
articles.body:
Syria has called for an “independent and transparent” investigation into the sinking of a cargo ship in the Black Sea, demanding answers over the fate of the ship’s 10 crew members, including nine Syrians and an Egyptian, who remain unaccounted for.

The Togolese-flagged Alfa Watan, went down in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone early on Tuesday, amid a rising number of drone strikes hitting Black Sea shipping during the Russia-Ukraine war.

It is unclear who carried out the attack.

Mazen Aloush, from the Syria’s port authority asked the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and Bulgarian authorities to find out why a search and rescue mission was called off, before the missing sailors were found.

“Their fate is still unknown” said Aloush, adding that “the reasons that led to the suspension of search and rescue operations” had to be established.

The attack on Tuesday also hit the Palau-flagged Able, setting it ablaze. Eighteen Turkish and Indian crew members were rescued from the burning vessel, while the Alfa Watan sank.

Both commercial ships were managed by Turkey-based companies, according to the Equasis merchant shipping database.

The Syrian sailors’ union said contact with the ship’s crew had been lost and no survivors had been found after search operations were halted.

Aloush condemned the targeting of a civilian commercial vessel saying it was a serious breach of maritime security and a threat to sailors.

He said Syrian General Authority for Ports and Customs was closely monitoring the incident.

He urged ⁠authorities to use all available technical means to locate and inspect the wreckage to help establish what caused the ship to sink.

He called for international and maritime bodies to strengthen measures to help commercial shipping as attacks in the Black Sea rise.

articles.title: Black and African cinema hub opens in London
articles.summary: EbonyLife Place London is the brainchild of Nollywood media mogul Mo Abudu.
articles.body:
A new black and African cinema and hub has officially opened in south-west London.

EbonyLife Place, based near Nine Elms, was unveiled with a ceremony attended by the Mayor of London Lord Khan, and its founder Mo Abudu.

Abudu, a Nigerian media mogul who was born in London, explained that the project was born from a desire to showcase and celebrate stories that she felt previously lacked a home.

"I do think there is a younger audience of young people now that just want to see great storytelling," Abudu said.

She added: "We make great films, and I think we need to create experiences where people can come and they can see the great work that we do in black cinema, in African cinema.

"We don't have enough spaces to serve black cinema in the United Kingdom... representation is so important to us."

At the heart of the cultural centre is a 160-seat auditorium featuring a year-round film programme.

The screenings will primarily focus on Nollywood cinema from Nigeria alongside other movies connecting to the black experience.

In addition to film screenings, the venue will host masterclasses, industry panels, and live performances by established and emerging talent.

Beyond its cinema space, the multi-storey venue features a bar, a lounge called "Fàhinti" (a Yoruba word meaning to lean back and rest), a Nigerian restaurant, a boutique showcasing African and diaspora designers, and walls lined with African diaspora artwork.

The project, financed almost entirely by Abudu's media group, mirrors the upscale lifestyle complex she launched in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos, in 2019.

Speaking at Thursday's launch, Lord Khan said: "London is the number one place in Europe to film," adding that the capital sits just behind Los Angeles and ahead of New York in the global film production footprint.

"As long as I'm mayor, we'll invest in culture," he said.

The opening coincides with the London Film Festival.

articles.summary: Jordan Dupree Collins Sr. was convicted of second-degree murder after his teen son's remains were recovered from an Elk River landfill.
articles.body: A Minnesota man was found guilty of killing his teenage son, whose remains were found in a landfill after he vanished for over a month. Jordan Dupree Collins Sr., who represented himself during his trial, was convicted Wednesday of second-degree murder for killing his 16-year-old son, Jordan "Manny" Collins. Ashley Berry, the boy's mother, has previously described Manny as someone who was "always helping others, spreading kindness, and lifting up those around him." "Manny should still be here today," Anoka County Sheriff Brad Wise said in a statement. "No verdict can remove the pain his loved ones feel, but we hope this decision provides some measure of justice. Our thoughts remain with Manny’s family, especially his mother, Ashley, as they continue to grieve and remember him." MINNESOTA MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING MALL OF AMERICA ATTACK, PLEDGING ALLEGIANCE TO ISIS: FBI According to the criminal complaint, the teen went to his father's apartment in May 2025 and was never heard from again. His mother and his girlfriend both told police they last communicated with him in the early morning hours of May 8, 2025. Collins told Manny's mother that the 16-year-old left his Columbia Heights apartment on the afternoon of May 8 to go to St. Paul to visit his girlfriend and grandmother. The girlfriend later told authorities that Manny never indicated he was coming to visit during their last video call together. On May 15, 2025, police obtained a search warrant and descended on Collins' apartment, where they found "items with apparent blood staining in garbage bags in a living room closet." MAN KILLS WIFE AND 7-YEAR-OLD DAUGHTER BEFORE TAKING OWN LIFE AT MINNESOTA HOME DAYCARE; FOURTH VICTIM FOUND Police said DNA testing confirmed that the blood found in the apartment belonged to Manny. articles.title: Woman told Merseyside PC 'get off me' 300 times as he raped her
articles.summary: Ryan Theaker, 30, was secretly recorded by the victim as he subjected her to an 82 minute attack.
articles.body:
A woman told a police officer to "get off me" more than 300 times as he subjected her to an 82-minute violent rape in a Liverpool hotel room.

Former Merseyside Police constable Ryan Theaker, 30, was secretly recorded by the victim after a night out in 2023.

The woman, who cannot be named to protect her anonymity, read an emotional statement at Liverpool Crown Court and faced the dock as she told Theaker "monsters never win".

He was designated a "dangerous" offender by a judge and jailed for 11 years with an extended five-year licence period.

Warning: This story contains distressing details of sexual violence.

Theaker, from Park Lane in Netherton, had been convicted of rape, sexual assault and assault by penetration after a trial last month.

Gareth Roberts, prosecuting, said the audio recordings captured Theaker demanding the woman let him take naked pictures of her, despite her saying she did not want him to.

He also assaulted her with sex toys he had brought to the hotel, the court heard.

The recordings, described as "harrowing" by sentencing judge Brian Cummings KC, captured her "crying throughout" as Theaker went on to rape her.

Theaker, who was off duty at the time, was heard to tell her: "It'll stop when I say."

Roberts summarised the attack as a "lengthy and prolonged period of sexual degradation".

The offences were reported about a year later, after the victim confided in family and friends following a "serious" suicide attempt.

The woman was invited to read her victim personal statement aloud and wiped away tears as she said: "I always thought when I was younger that monsters were big horrible nasty creatures who weren't even real.

"I remember reading a post that said, 'even Scooby doo taught us the real monsters were always the people'.

"That is exactly what he is. A monster. The monster never wins."

She also said she could not understand how he could have arrested people after "doing what he did to me" and "still been proud to wear that uniform".

"He didn't deserve to be in the police," she added.

Theaker did not appear to react as she read her statement and the woman was embraced and supported by her family as she returned to the public gallery.

Jenny Tallentire, defending, said since the trial Theaker had accepted he was guilty of the sexual offences and was "ashamed" of his behaviour.

She said he had been an "excellent" police officer who had been commended and nominated for a bravery award during his career.

Outlining Theaker's crimes as he passed sentence, Judge Cummings said: "You repeatedly told her get in the [expletive] bath which she refused to do, pushed her on the bed, removed her clothing and took photographs of her despite her repeatedly telling you she didn't want you to."

He said he forced her to wear sexual restraints and assaulted her.

Just as she thought the ordeal was over, the judge said Theaker grabbed her by the hair and raped her.

Judge Cummings said he took into account Theaker's public service and acknowledged that his status as a police officer would put him at increased risk in custody.

However, he said: "I am quite sure that your behaviour towards the victim across the offences made at the very least a substantial contribution to her decision to try and kill herself."

After the offences were reported in August 2024, Theaker was suspended and subjected to misconduct proceedings.

He resigned the day before a hearing in August 2025, which concluded he would have been sacked had he remained on the force.

After the sentencing Merseyside Police Assistant Chief Constable Karen Jaundrill said: "The behaviour for which Theaker has been convicted and sentenced has no place in society, and certainly not within policing.

"I want to be clear that his contemptible behaviour is in no way representative of the attitude or behaviour of officers and staff at Merseyside Police.

"Theaker's former colleagues, and the force, have all been left shocked and disgusted by his actions and the long-term impact they have had on his victim."

articles.title: Hurricane Isaias charges towards the US Gulf Coast with dangerous winds
articles.summary: The storm is forecast to strike Florida, Alabama and Mississippi with up to 10 inches of rain this weekend.
articles.body:
Hurricane Isaias has intensified into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season as it barrels over record-warm water toward the northern shoreline of the United States Gulf Coast, prompting school closures and local government shutdowns.

According to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center, the storm is forecast to make landfall in parts of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi late Friday or early Saturday. The low-lying areas are especially vulnerable to flooding and storm surges.

The center warned residents in likely impact zones on Thursday to complete all emergency life-safety and property protections without delay.

It has also issued a hurricane watch from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, through Indian Pass in the northwestern part of Florida in anticipation of torrential downpours and the substantial risk of localised flash and urban flooding.

A rainfall total of 3-6 inches is forecast with isolated peaks up to 10 inches.

“We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said in a Thursday morning update, adding that he expects “up to near-major hurricane strength” by Friday as the storm pounds north of Mexico’s Yucatan Peninsula.

On Thursday morning, Isaias was packing maximum sustained winds of nearly 130km/h (80mph) with higher gusts. Heavy rain and flash flooding also threaten the inland areas throughout the weekend, extending as far as the Tennessee Valley and potentially encompassing a broad stretch from the inland southeast up through the southern Appalachian Mountains.

Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the US Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 percent of crude pumped annually in the US.

As of Wednesday, about 25 percent of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.

With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.

When Isaias was first declared a hurricane on Wednesday, it marked the latest date for an Atlantic season’s first hurricane in 121 years, falling just short of the record set in 1905, according to data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The season normally runs from June 1 through November 30.

articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — An upcoming documentary examines the lasting toll of school closures six years after the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted classrooms nationwide. "Generation COVID," directed by Jennifer Sey and Andrew James, follows children and families across California, New York, Oregon, Colorado and Connecticut as they grapple with the effects of pandemic-era school closures and mandates. The documentary was filmed over more than four years. Sey told Fox News Digital that while much of the country appears ready to move on from the pandemic, many children are still struggling with its consequences. NEWSOM'S ADMISSION THAT INFAMOUS COVID MOVE WAS 'INSANE' TRIGGERS VIRAL FURY: 'WE ALL TOLD YOU' "It just feels to me like everyone wants to move on, and there’s really been no reckoning about what we did to young people in particular, and I wanted to create a record of that so that it never happens again," the XX-XY Athletics founder said. Sey said she hopes the film offers a visual record of how school closures affected American children and encourages a different approach during any future pandemic. LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS Sey lived in San Francisco for more than three decades and spoke out against the city’s prolonged shutdowns. "I ended up having to leave San Francisco. I lost a career I'd spent 30 years building, but I continued to speak out in defense of children." After leaving her job in 2022, Sey began producing the documentary. Sey, a former elite gymnast and national team member, said her commitment to protecting children is rooted in the abuse she experienced as a young athlete. She is also an Emmy-winning producer of "Athlete A," a documentary examining the Larry Nassar sexual abuse scandal and broader abuse within elite gymnastics. "I ended up being the first whistleblower about abuse in elite gymnastics all the way back in 2008. And I really did it because I wish someone had stood up for me when I was a child. And the abuse that I suffered, I really did not come out of it for two decades after having left the sport. And, so, when I see that children are suffering, I can't help myself. I will fight for them. "I feel like everyone's moved on, but the kids have not moved on." Sey said her experiences have shaped her determination to continue speaking out for children. HERE'S HOW THE CDC TRIED TO USE BAD SCIENCE TO CONVINCE PEOPLE TO WEAR MASKS DURING COVID She also argued that children were "dehumanized" during the pandemic. "They were models, they were cogs in a wheel, and we lost all sense of the humanity of a child, the need to be around other kids for their own development. We lost a sense of a child learning to speak that's 3 years old and being told if you don't wear a mask, you're going to kill your grandmother. Who tells a child that? Who tells a small child that? We inflicted fear." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The film examines the consequences of school closures and the censorship that Sey believes helped keep them in place. articles.title: Sewage spills in Wales exceeded 800,000 hours last year, report claims
articles.summary: It is equivalent to a sewage discharge happening every five minutes, according to campaigners.
articles.body:
New figures show sewage was released into rivers, lakes and the sea around Wales for more than 800,000 hours last year.

The charity Surfers Against Sewage, which has analysed data from Wales' water companies, said there were more than 100,000 sewage discharges in 2025 - or one every five minutes.

The figures are down on the year before when sewage was discharged for more than 970,000 hours.

Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it had strengthened its approach as regulators through increased monitoring and tighter guidance, and had overseen "significant programmes of environmental investment" by water companies.

Surfers Against Sewage said part of the reason for the drop was the dry weather seen during the summer last year, but underinvestment and a lack of enforcement remained an issue.

In its annual assessment, it said since 2019 it had received 992 reports of sickness in Wales caused by sewage, with 215 of those coming in 2025.

It said the impact of those sickness reports led to more than 2,200 days off work.

According to the charity, sewage was discharged into Wales' designated bathing waters for a total of 35,669 hours over the year.

At Llyn Padarn, Gwynedd, despite the lake's designated bathing water being classified as "excellent" for water quality, discharges lasted 1,614 hours.

Rules allow a limited discharge of sewage in periods of excess rain, but environmental groups remain concerned the levels pose a threat to wildlife and a health risk to swimmers.

Giles Bristow, chief executive of Surfers Against Sewage, said last year's figures equated to a discharge every five minutes, which he called a "shocking statistic".

He pointed to 90 places that authorities have said are good places to swim, but said they'd "been impacted by over 4,000 hours of sewage pollution".

"It's a really terrible picture that we're seeing of continued underinvestment and a lack of enforcement to ensure that this isn't happening," he added.

"People's lives and their health are being put at risk when they go to enjoy these amazing places."

Welsh Water said it will invest a record £2.5bn over the next four years, and understood the concerns about sewage discharge.

"We take our responsibility to protect these waters seriously and recognise that we need to improve," it said.

"In line with Welsh government policy, we are prioritising the overflows causing the greatest environmental harm."

Hafren Dyfrdwy - which operates in mid and north-east Wales - said it was "working tirelessly" to reduce the average number of spills but "we know more needs to be done".

"Which is why we're investing £11m at our storm overflows to reduce spills to fewer than 20 a year by 2030," it added.

The Welsh government said it was "taking full control of water in Wales" and would "apply the polluter-pays principle, including prosecuting serious and persistent offenders".

"Water reform demonstrates how Wales and the UK can work together to strengthen and simplify devolution, while keeping effective cross-border cooperation," a spokesperson added.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said water companies must "take responsibility" for record levels of sewage pollution.

It added: "Our strengthened Water Bill will deliver cleaner waters, stronger accountability and will create a powerful new regulator to hold companies to account."

articles.title: Colombian embassy to open in Jerusalem, Israeli FM says
articles.summary: Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella had promised closer ties with Israel on the campaign trail.
articles.body:
Israel has announced that Colombia will open an embassy in Jerusalem, becoming the latest country to establish a diplomatic mission in the disputed city claimed as a capital by Israelis and Palestinians. Most countries have their embassies in Israel in Tel Aviv.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Thursday the Latin American country’s embassy would open next week as he touted expanding relations with the region.

“Next Wednesday, we are going to inaugurate … the Colombian embassy,” Saar told attendees at a conference in Jerusalem.

An official at the Colombian Foreign Ministry in Bogota told AFP news agency the country’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar would travel to Jerusalem on Sunday ahead of the opening.

Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella , who was sworn in as president in August, promised close relations with Israel during his election campaign. When he came into office, he restored diplomatic ties between Colombia and Israel. Colombia had previously severed ties with the country over Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.

The announcement comes as a small but growing list of countries has opted to route their diplomatic ties with Israel through Jerusalem.

Since 2018, the US, Guatemala, Paraguay, Kosovo, Honduras, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Nauru and Somaliland, which has been recognised as an independent entity only by Israel, have opened embassies in the city.

Other countries that have diplomatic relations with Israel have located their embassies in Tel Aviv, as Jerusalem is not recognised by the international community as Israel’s capital.

“We will work hard because this is the diplomatic battle over the truth. And the truth is, Jerusalem was always the capital of one nation,” Saar said, dismissing Palestinian claims to the capital.

The Israeli minister said the Democratic Republic of the Congo would open its embassy in Jerusalem “very soon” and hinted at another opening.

“I think that with the possible results in Brazil, they might have the same move,” he said after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro won the first round in the country’s presidential election.

Protesters in Colombia took to the streets of Bogota on Wednesday to rally against the new far-right government’s policy towards Israel, including the decision to open the Jerusalem embassy.

“When diplomatic relations with Israel were broken off, the message was that we would not be a nation complicit in their atrocities,” Nicolas Isaza, who took part in the protest, told Al Jazeera.

“Today our government is no longer drawing a line against the atrocities being committed in Palestine,” he added.

articles.title: E-bike battery in fatal fire had repairs, inquest hears
articles.summary: Gemma Germeney, 31, and children Lilly, eight, and Oliver, four, lost their lives in the blaze.
articles.body:
An e-bike battery linked to a fire which killed a mother and two children had issues prior to the blaze, an inquest has heard.

Gemma Germeney, 31, and children Lilly, eight, and Oliver, four, lost their lives in the fire on Sackville Close in Cambridge on 30 June 2023. The children's father, Scott Peden, survived.

Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service said at the time the most probable cause of the fire was an e-bike that was charging.

Scott Peden told the inquest he had bought a replacement battery after the previous one had been stolen and the bike later cut out, and had visited a repairman twice for work done.

Peden told the inquest he had purchased the bike online for £900 and it was in "perfect working order", apart from an incident where he lost the key on a fairground ride.

He said the battery was stolen a few months later and they researched a new one, but it would have been "quite a lot of money and I couldn't afford it at the time".

Peden told the inquest he bought a second-hand one online advertised as in "perfect working order" around 9 June.

He said the replacement "seemed to take a while to charge", but "it was getting enough for me to get around", however, it then "cut out" near his home.

A colleague had given them the details of repairman Stoil Severinov and he went with Germeney's father to his house, where he was told "the battery was too powerful for the fuse so he changed the fuse" for £30.

But he returned, this time alone, after it cut out again when he said Severinov told him the battery needed replacing, but Peden said he "had nothing in the bank, so I asked him desperately if he could do anything before I got paid".

He "offered to bypass the cells", and he was told this would be a temporary fix.

Asked if Severinov told him there were any risks, Peden replied "no".

Peden planned to "use the bike until payday" and said he paid £10 on the understanding he would return and purchase a new battery and charger.

He said on the night of the fire he heard a "massive bang" that went through the house, which was "very loud and very hard to miss".

Severinov, giving evidence through an interpreter, said he was repairing bikes and e-bikes.

He said on the first occasion Peden visited he changed the socket and the fuse, and on the second "it was just the fuse".

On the first occasion he had explained "it was a temporary fix".

Severinov said he remembered telling Peden he needed a new battery, and said he had "never done anything to the battery cells", adding he "didn't have the expertise in the first place".

The court heard Severinov was interviewed under caution by the Office for Product Safety and Standards, which has primacy in bringing any criminal proceedings in this case.

It was told it had said no final decision had been made on whether to initiate criminal proceedings against any individuals or organisations.

A pen portrait from Germeney's mother, read out at the beginning of the inquest by the coroner, said Germeney and the children were "our complete world" and "were beautiful, funny, extremely kind, loving and caring".

articles.title: Israel opens first-ever pavilion at Morocco defence show
articles.summary: Israel opened its first national pavilion at Morocco’s Marrakech Air Show, joined by Israel’s top military contractors.
articles.body:
Israel’s Ministry of Defence says it is participating for the first time in a defence exhibition in Morocco, as it announced its first-ever national pavilion at the Marrakesh Air Show 2026.

“This marks Israel’s first official participation in the defence exhibition held in Morocco since the signing of the Abraham Accords”, Israel’s Defence Ministry said in a statement on Thursday.

The ministry said eight Israeli defence companies exhibited “advanced, combat-proven technologies at the show” in Marrakesh, which runs until Saturday.

The Marrakech Air Show, taking place from October 7 to October 10 this year at the Marrakech Royal Moroccan Air Force Base, is organised every two years and is meant for civil and military aeronautics and space industries to highlight their latest offerings.

“Israel’s three major defence industries, Elbit Systems, IAI, and Rafael, also exhibited, presenting solutions across the air, land, sea, space, intelligence, cyber, and digital domains,” it said.

The announcement is the latest sign of increasing ties between the Arabic-speaking North African country and Israel, since the two established ties in 2020 as part of the US-backed Abraham Accords.

Last month, Israel and Morocco agreed to upgrade their diplomatic ties, including elevating their respective missions to embassies and appointing ambassadors to both countries.

The move followed a meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers, hosted by the US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

They also agreed to expand air travel, including by reinstating direct flights operated by carriers from both nations, and confirmed plans for high-level bilateral visits in the coming months.

Morocco is also one of the five countries that have pledged to send troops to Gaza, under the US-backed International Stabilization Force (ISF) as part of US President Donald Trump’s so-called Board of Peace.

articles.title: Prison officer and inmate sent 5,000 Snapchat messages in fling
articles.summary: Former prison officer Jade Morris and drug dealer Jerome Nunes will be sentenced on Friday.
articles.body:
A prison officer and inmate shared more than 5,000 illicit Snapchat messages during a secret fling, a court has heard.

Jade Morris, from Holmer in Herefordshire, was discovered to be having a relationship with convicted drug dealer Jerome Nunes, 35, after he flung a banned mobile phone out of a cell window in October 2022.

The 37-year-old former custody officer, who worked in the maximum-security unit at HMP Long Lartin in Worcestershire, also exchanged dozens of WhatsApp messages with Nunes, a sentencing hearing was told.

She pleaded guilty at a hearing in March to offences of misconduct in public office and encouraging Nunes to use a prohibited device. Both are set to be sentenced on Friday.

Opening the facts of the case at Birmingham Crown Court on Thursday, prosecutor Cathlyn Orchard said Nunes, from Newport, South Wales, had 23 previous convictions and was serving a sentence for a drugs conspiracy offence.

The court heard Nunes had been subject to a cell search in October 2022, leading to the recovery of one of several phones used to communicate with Morris, mainly in the early hours.

Morris initially described the allegations against her as "ludicrous" and denied having any relationship with Nunes after being arrested at her home in January 2023.

Orchard told Judge Peter Carr that the former prison officer had saved the prisoner's number as Ghost in her phone's contacts.

Further inquiries recovered evidence of Snapchat calls and messages and Morris was interviewed again in May 2024, when she admitted communicating with a prisoner who she refused to name, claiming to have been feeling intimidated and frightened.

When describing deleted material and messages recovered during the inquiry, including a letter found on Nunes's phone, the prosecutor told the judge: "It seems implicit that they must have been sharing sexual images."

Nunes pleaded guilty at Birmingham Magistrates' Court in February 2026 to two offences under the Prison Act 1952 for possessing and using an unauthorised mobile phone.

Mitigating barrister Holly Sims, arguing that Morris could be dealt with by a suspended sentence, said: "There is no evidence of any physical contact or of explicit photos being shared between either of the two defendants.

"It is of course conceded that these offences are serious.

"She is extremely ashamed and embarrassed of her behaviour."

Mitigating lawyer Matthew Bolt argued Nunes, who was freed nearly two years ago, could be spared an immediate prison sentenced - describing him as a "man in a hurry" who was running a small food business.

Both defendants, who had been on bail, were remanded in custody overnight ahead of their sentencing.

articles.title: Maryland man accused of girl's fatal shooting released from prison days before
articles.summary: Tyree Reynolds was released from prison just eight days before allegedly killing 12-year-old Khloe Ishway near a Baltimore youth football game.
articles.body: A Maryland man charged with killing a 12-year-old girl while allegedly firing at two men near a youth football game was released from prison just eight days before the deadly shooting. Tyree Reynolds, 23, was released from state custody on Sept. 25, according to Fox 45 News, which cited the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (MDPSCS). Reynolds faces 30 criminal counts, including murder and attempted murder, in connection with Saturday's shooting at a youth football homecoming game at Leon Day Park in Baltimore. HOUSE DEMOCRAT BLASTED AFTER EARLY RELEASE LAW FREED INMATES LATER CHARGED WITH MURDER During a Wednesday court appearance, Reynolds waived his bond hearing. He appeared via video from a wheelchair with a cast around his leg. Authorities said surveillance footage captured Reynolds opening fire on two men in a parking lot adjacent to the football field during an argument over a parking spot. Investigators allege Reynolds reached into a backpack, pulled out a short-barreled rifle and began firing. POLICE MAKE ARREST AFTER GUNFIRE DURING CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL GAME LEAVES 1 DEAD One of the men returned fire, striking Reynolds in the ankle. Reynolds then allegedly fired toward the football field, striking 12-year-old Khloe Ishway and three other victims. Ishway died from her injuries. "Khloe was just 12 years old. She should have a whole life ahead of her: school, a career, time spent with family and friends. Instead, she was killed because two adult men resorted to deadly violence to resolve an argument over a parking spot," Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said. "Our hearts remain with Khloe's mother, her family and friends, and our entire community, and we are committed to getting justice on their behalf," he continued. CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM At the time of the shooting, Reynolds was on probation stemming from a previous shooting for which he had recently completed his prison sentence. "The Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services is heartbroken by the tragic death of 12-year-old Khloe Ishway and the injuries to innocent bystanders," the agency said in a statement. "Tyree Reynolds was previously sentenced to 15 years of incarceration, with all but five years suspended by a judge. Reynolds served the entirety of that five-year term, day for day, and was released on September 25, 2026." Reynolds was arrested three times in 2021. In February of that year, he was arrested on a handgun possession charge and was granted pretrial release. Reynolds later pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of first-degree assault and a firearms violation. He was sentenced to 15 years in prison, followed by three years of probation. A judge suspended all but five years of the 15-year sentence, which Reynolds served in full before his release in September.

articles.title: Harry says he 'slipped into depression' after leaving UK for Canada
articles.summary: The Duke of Sussex says he had an "adrenaline crash" while visiting Vancouver Island to "get some space".
articles.body:
The Duke of Sussex has said he "slipped into depression for about two weeks" after relocating to Canada in 2019 ahead of his move to the US.

Prince Harry, who recently returned to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children, said he had originally left the country to "get some space."

The duke also discussed feeling "emotionally numb" after the death of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales, because he felt "disloyal and guilty for the possibility of being happy and joyful without her".

He opened up about his mental health with a neuroscientist in a session for a video learning platform.

He and his brother, the Prince of Wales, have previously been candid about their mental health struggles, including over their mother's death, and both are involved in mental health charities.

Prince Harry, who stepped back from royal duties to move to California with Meghan, made the latest comments as part of a paid-for online masterclass on dealing with grief.

"Being in Canada, away from the stressful environment where presumably my body was just pumped full of adrenaline, within two or three days, I experienced this adrenaline crash, something that I'd never experienced before," he recalled.

"It was as if I needed stress in order to get the adrenaline to make my brain function because I became useless around the house.

"I actually slipped into depression for about two weeks and I felt like I couldn't function without adrenaline."

Prince Harry says it is 'great' to be back in Britain after six years in US

Will Harry's return heal deep-rooted rift with William?

He and his wife unexpectedly announced last month that they were returning to the UK with their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, after spending six years in the US. They are now thought to be living in the Cotswolds.

In the video, Prince Harry also revealed that he had a rule that he would never be away from his family for more than 10 days.

He talked about struggling to process his grief in the years after the death of his mother when he was 12.

"In my 20s, I went to war twice thinking I could outrun my feelings," the duke said, referring to his stints in Afghanistan as a member of the Army. "But that's not what happened.

"I'd spent so long emotionally numb, to a large extent, because I felt disloyal and guilty for the possibility of being happy and joyful without her.

"I felt like I had to be sad and I had to be emotionally numb in order to prove to her that I missed her."

Prince Harry said in the discussion that after crying at Diana's funeral, he did not cry for nearly two decades, according to news outlets.

He said it was a therapist who suggested he spray her perfume to "unlock everything", adding that this allowed him to discover that "she just wanted me to be happy".

Mary-Frances O'Connor, a neuroscientist and University of Arizona professor who also featured in the online class, explained: "Your brain doesn't register your loved one as gone - it registers them as lost.

"And it will keep searching until you teach it otherwise. We still expect that they're going to walk through the door."

MasterClass approached Harry about appearing in the programme last year and it was filmed in California over the summer, according to People magazine.

articles.title: Jon Stewart tells Democrats to 'govern' and skip 'performative' Trump impeachment if they win
articles.summary: Jon Stewart warned Democrats against the "performative play" of impeaching President Donald Trump, urging the party to govern and fix the issues killing people now.
articles.body: Comedian Jon Stewart urged Democrats not to pursue impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump if they regain control of the House and Senate, arguing on his podcast that he doesn't want to see "performative" hearings. During a question-and-answer segment at the end of Stewart's "The Weekly Show" podcast, he was asked whether Democrats should seek to impeach Trump if they regain control of Congress in the midterm elections. He said he wanted to see Democrats make a full-scale effort to rebalance the economy, and said he didn't want to see performative hearings. "I don't want to see a f---ing five-act performative play of House hearings," Stewart said. "I just don't want to see it. I don't want to see everybody having the opportunity to pantomime accountability because you know they're actually not going to bring it." STEWART EXPECTS SCHUMER, JEFFRIES TO DISAPPOINT IF THE DEMS WIN BACK THE HOUSE AND SENATE "You want to do some investigations of some s---, that's great," he continued. "But on the triage list of what's wrong in this country, it is, 'I'm sorry, sir, you're going to have to stay in the waiting room because this guy just got shot, and it sounds to me like you just have a sore throat.' Like do the s--- that actually is killing people right now." Stewart added that he wanted Democrats to "govern." "You want to do some things that are ancillary, a little side project, you want to do the investigations as a hobby, knock yourself out. Fix s---," he said. "Jon Stewart is tapping into a real tension within the Democratic electorate," Lauryn Killian, CEO of Killian Campaigns, told Fox News Digital in a statement. "There will certainly be Democrats who want impeachment, particularly those who believe the Trump administration warrants aggressive congressional scrutiny." "But there is a meaningful difference between legitimate accountability and turning impeachment into another chapter of the anti-Trump resistance movement," she continued. "If Democrats take back Congress, voters will expect them to actually govern, not spend two years trying to undo the last election." HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY Killian said the smarter political strategy would be to look into "wrongdoing and pursue accountability where the facts warrant it, while focusing congressional energy on issues that actually affect Americans' lives: the economy, affordability, public safety and government competence." "Winning Congress would give Democrats an opportunity to demonstrate they can govern beyond simply being the opposition," she added. "If they turn that opportunity into another impeachment crusade, Republicans will have a very clear argument to make to voters: Democrats were given power to govern, and chose instead to keep fighting the last election." "Jon Stewart is saying what Democrats don't want to hear: voters want results, not revenge," Y. David Scharf, chair of government strategies and controversies at Morrison Cohen, told Fox News Digital. "If Democrats win Congress and spend the next two years trying to impeach Trump instead of lowering costs and fixing the economy, they'll be writing the Republican playbook for 2028." He described impeachment as "political theater." Democratic strategist James Carville and his podcast co-host Al Hunt also warned against impeachment on Tuesday. Carville and Hunt argued that impeachment would be a waste of time and Democrats should devote their energy to investigating the president instead. CARVILLE SAYS THE GOP IS BETTER THAN DEMOCRATS AT ONE KEY SKILL THE 2028 DEM NOMINEE WILL NEED "I’ll tell you one thing that I think Democrats should steer clear of, and that’s impeachment," Hunt said. "It’s not that Trump has not committed impeachable offenses, far worse than what he was accused of back in 2019 with Ukraine. I mean, he has. I mean, you could come up with a bill of particulars of, you know, a dozen at least. But you know something, James? It’s not going to happen, and it is a distraction." "It is a waste of energy," Hunt added. "Investigate, investigate, investigate. Don’t go on a mission that isn’t going to succeed." Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who also served as White House chief of staff, urged fellow Democrats not to pursue impeachment during an interview on Sunday. "You’re never going to get an impeachment," he said. "Then, if you do that, you just basically prove all [of] Washington is what the American people think. It’s Disneyland on the Potomac. Deliver the change. Deliver a comprehensive ethics package that uses the investigations to then deliver change." The warnings came as Democrats held a polling advantage over Republicans heading into the final weeks before the midterm elections. FORMER CHICAGO MAYOR RAHM EMANUEL DECLARES AMERICA IS READY FOR A JEWISH PRESIDENT House race projections show Democrats winning 215 seats compared to 201 for the GOP, meaning Democrats would need to win at least three of the 19 remaining toss-up races to clinch a majority. Republicans would need to win at least 17 of those races. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has declined to say whether he would support impeachment proceedings against Trump, though he appeared to suggest over the summer that impeachment would not be a top priority. articles.title: Group 'guarding' derelict Bridgwater cinema told to leave
articles.summary: The occupiers claimed they were protecting the abandoned building from thieves and vandals.
articles.body:
A group of people occupying an abandoned cinema to "guard" it from thieves and vandals have been ordered to leave the historic property.

Two defendants, Dean and Alex, who did not give their surnames, told a hearing at Taunton County Court on Wednesday that between 15 and 20 people were in the Bridgwater building "at any one time".

The occupiers moved into the property, which has been vacant since 2022, in March and Dean, 57, said they had been completing repairs and helping to deter anti-social behaviour.

Making the eviction order requested by the owner, Orlieu Solutions Limited, the judge said "no one else has the right to occupy other than the claimant". The owner declined to comment.

The ruling means that if the group refuses to leave, bailiffs can intervene and physically remove them.

Though squatting in residential buildings is a criminal offence, police cannot take action against squatters in non-residential buildings unless they commit a crime.

The last companies to operate in the Art Deco building before its closure were Scott Cinemas and Mecca Bingo.

In June, Somerset Council gave the current owner a formal notice to make the site safe.

At the time, the council said: "We have made a number of attempts to contact the owner, but have not yet received a response."

Dean and his fellow occupiers claimed that work was not completed, and any emergency renovations were carried out by themselves.

Bridgwater History and Civic Society, which supports the occupiers, sent a letter to the court ahead of the hearing.

In it, member Rodney Coate said: "It would be a great shame, and a historic loss to the town, if an eviction order is granted today, with the almost certain result that, without the current responsible occupier, vandals will enter the building and set fire to it."

He added that the occupier "is not a homeless person" but "has decided to take on the role of interim caretaker to try and save the building so that a future restoration and community use can be considered".

However, the judge said: "I have no choice but to give the possession order to the claimants."

Following the hearing, Dean told the BBC: "We just wanted to protect the space because we could see by all the bricked-up windows that nobody was looking after it.

"There's not much of that kind of thing left anymore, so I think some of it should be preserved so that people can see our heritage and history."

He added: "Our plan is to resist the eviction peacefully and see if that gives us a bit more time to get it registered as an Asset of Community Value, to bring more awareness to the building and gather support."

articles.title: Philippines ex-President Duterte fit to stand trial, ICC rules
articles.summary: The former president is able to understand the charges and follow the proceedings, panel of experts find.
articles.body:
Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have found former Philippine President Rodrigo ⁠Duterte fit to stand trial and able to face charges of crimes against humanity related to the so-called “ war on drugs ” he waged while in office.

The ex-leader is accused of murder and attempted murder for his alleged involvement in dozens of killings. He denies the charges, but faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.

The court in The Hague said on Thursday that independent medical experts had examined the 81-year-old’s health and concluded he was mentally fit to understand evidence and discuss his defence with his lawyers.

“The chamber was satisfied that the accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings,” the court said.

His legal team had previously attempted to get the case thrown out on medical grounds, arguing that serious memory loss had left him unable to absorb new information or reliably recall the past.

The trial is scheduled to open on November 30.

Duterte, who served as president from 2016 to 2022, was arrested in the Philippines in March 2025 and sent to the ICC’s headquarters in The Hague following a lengthy ICC investigation.

Last month, he appeared in person for the first time at the ICC.

Duterte denies the charges against him, saying he only ordered police to act in self-defence as part of his anti-drugs offensive. Judges also denied a request for him to be released from custody.

Estimates of the death toll in the crackdown on drugs during his presidential term vary, from the more than 6,000 reported by the national police to up to 30,000 claimed by human rights groups.

Prosecutors say that police and government hit squads carried out dozens of killings at his orders, motivated by the promise of money or to avoid becoming targets themselves.

Throughout his presidency, Duterte enjoyed a high approval rating from the public, allowing him to push for his brutal anti-drugs agenda.

He became the first Asian ex-leader to be arrested by the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world’s worst crimes, such as war crimes and crimes against humanity.

articles.title: ‘War lives in me’: Gaza playwright Ali Abu Yasin wins English PEN award
articles.summary: Honoured for his artistic resilience, Ali Abu Yasin continued writing for theatre amid the rubble.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – Ali Abu Yassin, a playwright from Gaza who continued writing even as Israel’s genocidal campaign devastated the world around him, has won a prestigious award in London.

“This prize is great not only for me, but for Gaza, Palestine, and all the Palestinian people,” Ali Abu Yasin, who was named on Thursday as “Writer of Courage 2026” by the literary group English PEN, told Al Jazeera.

The 62-year-old began writing plays and mastering the oud as a teenager in al-Shati refugee camp in Gaza, one of the largest in the Strip and a target of recent attacks.

“It’s how I was born, I’ve wanted to express myself using art since my childhood,” he told Al Jazeera.

After the war began in October, 2023, Abu Yasin stopped writing plays and instead wrote about life under Israeli bombardment.

Abu Yasin said for the first two years, he wrote about the situation in Gaza as Palestinians fled and feared for their lives.

“There was no theatre; it was impossible to have a theatre because Gaza was being destroyed,” the writer said, shaking his head.

Since 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza and the majority of survivors have been displaced several times over.

Abu Yasin works with actors who now rehearse their lines in makeshift tents, against the sound of gunfire.

“I was near death four, five times. I saw people around me die. We lived by chance, and those who died, died by chance,” Abu Yasin told Al Jazeera.

“My son was trapped under rubble; my house was bombed. So, during those two years, I was trying just to provide some safety to my family. To protect them from famine. And to document what was happening, so the world can hear my voice before I die.”

After a break, he wrote several screenplays that he hid and carried with him throughout displacement.

In 2004, Abu Yasin began working with the Said Al-Mishal Theatre, a hub for Palestinian culture in Gaza City that was levelled in a 2018 Israeli bombing.

Leading playwrights and theatre directors described the attack as “obliteration of this symbol of Palestinian culture and identity” in a letter to The Guardian newspaper.

In 2008, Abu Yasin began writing the Gaza Monologues, a series illustrating life in Gaza, both moments of joy and of pain.

A few weeks ago, Abu Yasin left Gaza with the support of an artist residency programme in France.

“I didn’t actually leave the war. The war lives in me, Gaza lives in me,” he said.

He has found himself conserving small amounts of water and minimising waste, habits he developed by living through the humanitarian crisis.

The award ceremony aligns with his trip to France, allowing him to attend in person largely by fortunate coincidence. For English PEN, the privilege of an in-person ceremony at the British Library is not taken for granted.

“For many years, writers living in Gaza have been among those with the most limited freedom of movement in the world. We recognise this and the direct impact it has on their freedom of expression,” an English PEN spokesperson told Al Jazeera.

Abu Yasin’s recent play, 50 Minutes , was shown in Gaza and tells the story of genocide and mourning. Actors rehearsed in a makeshift tent in a car park, many of them without any previous theatre experience.

Abu Yasin was nominated by the British academic and cultural critic Jacqueline Rose, who won the 2026 PEN Pinter Prize.

The Writer of Courage “is awarded to an author who is active in defence of freedom of expression, often at great risk to their own safety and liberty, and shares the PEN Pinter Prize with the winner,” says English PEN.

The organisation is the United Kingdom branch of PEN International, a global association of writers dedicated to “championing freedom of expression and literary advocacy worldwide”.

PEN America, its United States counterpart, came under fire in recent years as some alleged it did not support Palestinian writers. PEN America faced a boycott, leading to the resignation of its president in 2025.

English PEN, which operates independently from the US group, joined PEN International in calling for an arms embargo on Israel and condemning the killing of Palestinian writers.

Rose described his work as “a call for justice, a cry of outrage and a spiritual quest” in a press release.

“He has been the consistent chronicler of the harshness and cruelty of Palestinian existence, and the mentor of young people struggling to pluck meaning from the debris of their lives.”

Rose came to prominence with her 2005 book, The Question of Zion, a psychoanalysis of Zionism .

Abu Yasin has three children and 16 grandchildren. All are in Gaza except for his son, Amjad Abu Yasin, who is an actor in France.

“In Gaza, we have simple dreams. We want to live in peace and to live in freedom. We want the sky and the seas to be open,” he said. “We just want some freedom.”

articles.title: Work will not stop, whether I am here or not: Nana Patekar refused to look away from Maharashtra’s farm crisis
articles.summary: Nana Patekar’s NAAM Foundation aided Maharashtra farmers with drought relief, education support and flood rehabilitation, leaving a lasting rural legacy.
articles.body: Pune/Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar/Kolhapur: Everybody remembers Nana Patekar as the actor of thunderous monologues, piercing stares and charged silences. But far away from the arc lights, he spent years lending that same fierce intensity to a far greater cause — helping Maharashtra’s drought-scorched farming communities rebuild their lives.For Patekar — fondly called Nana — his deepest satisfaction didn’t come from cinema, but from helping the farmers.In an annual report of NAAM Foundation, the organisation he founded with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure in 2015, Patekar reflected on what truly mattered: “The greatest happiness came from going beyond oneself and doing something for another person. The work would never be finished. What mattered was the satisfaction of having tried hard. The rain would come too little, too much or at the wrong time. The problems would multiply, as the fight was with changing nature. But the work will not stop. Whether I am here or not.”Now, those words echo with a haunting resonance. The mission he believed would outlive him has become the strongest testament to his legacy.As drought and water scarcity continue to haunt Maharashtra, the state has lost a man who refused to see the farm crisis as someone else’s burden. He used his rare celebrity not to elevate himself, but to focus attention on the state’s most vulnerable section.For hundreds of families, Nana wasn’t a star. He was the helping hand that appeared when everything else seemed lost.The luxury car that never arrivedIt all began in 2015 when Nana was about to buy a luxury car and had even set aside Rs 1.5 crore. Then a late-night television report changed everything.It showed widows and children of farmers who had died by suicide. Shaken, he called his friend Anaspure. They split the car fund into cheques of Rs 15,000 each and gave them to the bereaved families. But the report kept haunting him. He realised charity could ease pain for a moment, but not end the crisis. That restlessness shaped his philanthropy — and turned one decision into a near folklore.What started as direct help became a larger mission — of water, education and rural rehabilitation.‘He held my daughter in his arms and gave us hope’Vimal Gaikwad from Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar was among the first women to receive help from NAAM Foundation. She was pregnant when her husband, a farmer crushed by drought and debt, died by suicide. “I was working as a farm worker when NAAM Foundation’s Sangita Kulkarni met me. She counselled me and told me all was not lost. Until then, nobody had spoken openly to me about my husband’s death,” Gaikwad recalled.She remembered her first meeting with Nana. “I met him when my daughter was only a month old. He held her in his arms. The foundation provided me with financial aid and helped me set up a flour mill. Eleven years later, that mill has allowed me to raise my children with dignity,” teary-eyed Gaikwad said.‘Nana changed the destiny of my family’For Vaibhav Kalyane (25) from drought-hit Latur, Nana’s intervention altered the course of his life. “The continuous drought meant our family struggled even for two square meals every day. NAAM Foundation sponsored my entire engineering education. Today, I work in an engineering firm in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar,” Kalyane, the first graduate in his family, said.“Even this year, the soybean crop on our 2.5-acre farm has failed. But as I have a stable job, my family doesn’t have to worry too much,” he said.‘It feels like losing a family member’Sachin Chavan (27) was just 14 when his father died by suicide in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. “The debt and failed crops destroyed our family. My elder brother had to abandon his education after Std XII. I would have met the same fate if NAAM Foundation had not stepped in,” he recalled.The foundation financed his engineering degree. Today, Chavan too works in the engineering sector. “When the news (of Nana’s passing) came, everyone in my office was saddened. Other actors entertained us, but Nana felt like family. For me, it feels like losing someone close all over again,” he said.Many of the students whose lives were transformed by NAAM Foundation now return as volunteers, helping others walk the same difficult path they once travelled.A lifeline after disasterWhen devastating floods submerged large parts of Kolhapur and Sangli in 2019, Nana showed up once again. Through NAAM Foundation, 40 truckloads of relief material, including food, clothes and tin sheets, were dispatched to affected areas. After the floodwaters receded, more than 4,000 volunteers helped villagers clear debris and rebuild shattered homes.Premila Bhokare from Danwad village still remembers meeting Nana at a rehabilitation camp. “I broke down when I saw him. We had lost almost everything,” she said.Nana listened quietly before replying. “You have lost nothing. Don’t cry over a house or utensils. Those can be built again,” Bhokare recalled Nana’s words, which were not mere consolation.“He helped rebuild the house. He ensured we got utensils, clothes, books and stationery for the children. Most people donate what they no longer need. Nana specifically asked people to donate new clothes, so disaster victims could preserve their dignity,” she said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolhapur | Silver Rate in Kolhapur | Bank Holidays in Kolhapur | Public Holidays in KolhapurStay updated with the latest Kolhapur news. articles.title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped and thinks it may have been a politically motivated attack
articles.summary: Bernadette Greene-Placentia said she was hit from behind and knocked unconscious before waking up to two men attacking her.
articles.body: A Democratic congressional candidate in Arizona said she was raped in August while out fixing campaign signs along a road in the Phoenix metropolitan area, and she thinks the attack may have been politically motivated. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, 52, told the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office that she was returning to her car around 2 a.m. on Aug. 14 in Sun City when she was struck in the back of the head and raped by a man, according to an incident report obtained by NBC News. She said a second man also climbed on top of her before she tried to fight him off. Greene-Placentia, who is challenging Republican Rep. Abe Hamadeh in Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, reported the alleged assault to authorities on Aug. 31, more than two weeks after she said it occurred. Greene-Placentia told police she believed her attackers recognized her as a political figure, according to the incident report. She told NBC News on Wednesday that she recalled hearing one of the suspects saying “ick b----,” which she said in her head filled in as “democratic b----.” “Bernadette also recalled one of the male suspects stating, “democratic b----,” at some point during the incident but she did not clarify or recall when this may have been said,” the incident report states. Greene-Placentia told NBC News that she had little memory of the moments leading up to the attack and did not hear anyone approach her. She said she was struck in the back of her head in a way that left a “huge lump.” When she regained consciousness on the ground, she said, one man was sexually assaulting her. She said she then tried to fight off a second man. Greene-Placentia said the second man said, “You’re right, she’s not worth it,” before they left, according to the incident report. She added that she does not recall the men’s faces or their appearances. “I don’t know how long I laid there. I don’t think it was very long,” she said. “And then I remember looking up, I guess I had rolled over, and my car was only like three yards away.” “All I can remember is their feet, their pant leg,” she later added. “It’s frustrating.” Her campaign manager confirmed to NBC News that Greene-Placentia and others on the campaign often go out in the middle of the night to repair and put out campaign signs to avoid the heat and traffic. Greene-Placentia said she returned home after the alleged attack but does not remember the drive. According to the incident report, she did not seek medical treatment or undergo a sexual assault forensic examination. She told police she took three showers and a bath immediately after the sexual assault. She told NBC News she initially kept the incident to herself because she was embarrassed that she was unable to defend herself — particularly given the years she spent learning how to protect herself when she was a long-haul truck driver. “I will tell you, I have pretty good situational awareness,” she said. “You’re not a woman in trucking without being aware of your surroundings. Somebody was pretty f---ing quiet, and they snuck up behind me and hit me on the back of the head.” Greene-Placentia said she told her husband and communications coordinator about the assault two to three days afterward, according to the incident report. Her husband and communications coordinator recounted to the Phoenix New Times how she told them what happened. “I never imagined that something like this would happen just, you know, miles from my house, and I was embarrassed. Like, ‘Oh my God, I couldn’t defend myself,’” she said. “So I didn’t want to tell anybody.” Her landlord, who asked to remain anonymous out of respect for her privacy, told NBC News she encountered an “extremely shaken” Greene-Placentia a few days after the alleged incident on the driveway as she was leaving to have dinner with a friend. She recalled Greene-Placentia was “visibly trembling” and “appeared as though she might have difficulty remaining on her feet.” “I asked her, ‘Are you OK?’ At that point, I saw her visibly compose herself and change her demeanor,” the landlord said. “She told me that she was upset about the lack of support she felt she was receiving from the Democratic Party. We had a brief conversation about that as she went into the garage to access her apartment.” The landlord added that she remembered being struck by how shaken Greene-Placentia had appeared and did not know what was causing that reaction. She added that she does not want to speculate on her state of mind or about anything she did not personally witness. “My concern is for Bernadette and for treating her with dignity and respect as she deals with an extraordinarily difficult experience,” she said. “I hope the focus remains on her well-being and on allowing the appropriate authorities to conduct their work.” Greene-Placentia explained to NBC News that she eventually decided to contact authorities after delivering a campaign speech to a group of seniors and found herself reflecting on her promise to advocate for others. “I couldn’t look people in the eye and say I’m going to fight for them if I’m not willing to fight for everybody,” she said. Greene-Placentia said the alleged attack also left her with bruises on her back and arms, and she has what appears to be finger marks where someone gripped her. She told police she didn’t take pictures of the bump on the back of her head or bruises, the incident report states. She said that the bruises were still visible by the time she spoke to investigators, but they did not take photographs. The Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office told NBC News on Wednesday that the investigation is ongoing. The office did not immediately respond to a request for an update or if any suspects have been identified on Thursday. The attorney general’s office declined to comment, telling NBC News it is not involved in this investigation. Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., responded to the news on Wednesday night, writing on X he is “heartbroken” and calling for those responsible to be held accountable. In a statement from her office, Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs said she is “outraged” by the alleged “cruel and cowardly attack, and it has no place in Arizona.” “No one should have to fear for their safety, or the safety of the people they love, while serving their community,” the statement said. “Violence of any kind, against anyone, will not be tolerated in our state. Our hearts are with Bernadette and her loved ones.” If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.
