articles.title: Nebraska Christian therapists sue city over ban on helping minors accept their biological sex
articles.summary: The Thomas More Society claims Lincoln, Nebraska's, ordinance threatens therapists with jail and fines for helping minors address unwanted same-sex attraction.
articles.body: Christian counselors are suing Lincoln, Nebraska, over an ordinance they say threatens therapists with jail, fines and professional consequences for helping minors who want to become comfortable with their biological sex or address unwanted same-sex attraction, even after the Supreme Court struck down a similar Colorado restriction earlier this year. Thomas More Society Senior Counsel Matt Heffron told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that Lincoln's ordinance amounts to government "viewpoint discrimination," arguing counselors are permitted to help minors move toward gender transition but are barred from counseling them toward accepting their biological sex when that is the client's stated goal. "The government allows certain type of speech in therapy sessions, and it disallows other sorts of speech or viewpoints," Heffron said. "It's just a confirmation of government viewpoint, government-favored speech over disfavored speech." FIRED SCHOOL COUNSELOR LOSES AGAIN AFTER FREE SPEECH FIGHT OVER GENDER-THEMED BOOKS IN HIS OFFICE Heffron said Lincoln's ordinance prevents counselors from helping minors who want to become comfortable with their biological sex or address unwanted same-sex attraction. He argued that a nearly identical Colorado restriction was found unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Chiles v. Salazar as viewpoint discrimination and that the 8th Circuit subsequently reached a similar conclusion in a case involving Kansas City. EXCLUSIVE: INDIANA SCHOOL COUNSELOR FIRED FOR SPEAKING OUT ON GENDER IDENTITY POLICY SETTLES LAWSUIT FOR $200K Heffron said a counselor accused of having those conversations could face an investigation and potentially a misdemeanor charge, a $500 fine, a $100 civil penalty and the loss of professional licenses or credentials. Heffron said the Thomas More Society repeatedly asked Lincoln to repeal the ordinance or agree not to enforce it. So, after the city declined to do so and stopped responding, the group filed suit. DETRANSITIONERS REVEAL HOW DOCTORS PUSHED THEM TOWARD LIFE-ALTERING TREATMENT AS TEENS "The stakes of this case, as far as minors are concerned, is that there are minors out there, and a fair number of them is what I hear, who are, perhaps faith-based or for other reasons, they are unhappy with same-sex attraction that they may be experiencing, or they're unhappy with what used to be called gender dysphoria," Heffron said. "And these minors go to a therapist, particularly a Catholic one like the one in this case, and they ask to be helped. It's awful. It's cruel to tell those children they can't be helped. "In fact, the only thing that the statute or that ordinance allows is it will allow that therapist to help guide them into gender transition with all of the evils that include surgeries and hormones and that sort of thing. They can guide them into that. And they can make them comfortable with their same-sex attraction." CATHOLIC NUNS CARING FOR DYING PATIENTS FIGHT NEW YORK TRANS RULE, FACE JAIL TIME In this instance, Heffron said the government is policing speech. "When an ordinance tries to say what sort of view is allowed, what sort of speech is allowed, that's viewpoint discrimination," Heffron said. The city said that it does not comment on pending litigation.

articles.title: Thousands bid final goodbye to Natsamrat at Donje farmhouse near Khadakwasla
articles.summary: Veteran actor Nana Patekar, 75, cremated with full state honours at his Donje farmhouse near Khadakwasla; son Malhar performed rites as thousands paid respects.
articles.body: Pune: Veteran actor Nana Patekar (75) was cremated with full state honours on Thursday night on a quiet patch of land beside his farmhouse, Nanachi Wadi, in Donje near Khadakwasla, in accordance with his wishes. The choice of location reflected his bond with nature and his preference for a simple, private life away from the spotlight.Preparations for the cremation began early, as workers built the funeral pyre with wood from Patekar’s own farm, honouring a wish he had expressed years earlier. By evening, the once-quiet expanse had become the setting for one of Maharashtra’s most poignant farewells. His son, Malhar, performed the final rites and lit the pyre.Authorities restricted access to the farmhouse from around 2pm, permitting entry only to pedestrians and vehicles carrying dignitaries. As the day progressed, large crowds gathered outside the property, lining the barricaded roads for a final glimpse of the actor who remained closely connected to his roots throughout his life.Separate arrangements were made for VIPs and members of the public, while giant screens were installed to allow mourners outside the venue to witness the final rites. State cabinet minister Chandrakant Patil arrived early and remained at the site throughout the evening. Among the first from the film fraternity to pay their respects was actor Pravin Tarde, a close associate of Patekar, followed by composer Rahul Ranade, NCP leader Rupali Chakankar and several other prominent personalities.As night fell, the atmosphere grew increasingly emotional. Hundreds who had assembled since the afternoon waited patiently as officials repeatedly appealed for calm. Shortly after 10pm, Patekar’s mortal remains arrived amid the sounds of cymbals, drums and trumpets. Chants from grieving admirers echoed through the venue before a solemn silence descended as the final rituals began.Several politicians attended the cremation, including former state cabinet minister and MLA Dhananjay Munde, deputy chief ministers Eknath Shinde and Sunetra Pawar, Maharashtra minister for industries, investment and services Uday Samant, Union minister of state for social justice and empowerment Ramdas Athawale, and Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration commissioner Tukaram Mundhe.Late into the night, the lights of Nanachi Wadi flickered against the Khadakwasla hillside as thousands stood in silent remembrance, bringing an end to a day-long vigil for one of Marathi and Indian cinema’s most respected and uncompromising voices.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: A woman paid about £80 for a Dior bag in a Cotswolds charity shop without knowing if it was genuine; experts identified it as a rare 2003 Koi Saddle Bag, and it later sold for £7,870
articles.summary: A woman discovered a rare 2003 Dior Koi Saddle Bag in a charity shop for £80, which fetched an incredible £7,870 at auction after being verified by experts as a limited-edition piece.
articles.body: A Dior handbag bought for about £80 in a Cotswolds charity shop has sold for £7,870 at auction in Moreton-in-Marsh.The woman had picked up the bag because she liked its design, without knowing whether it was genuine. She later took it to Kinghams auction house, where specialists identified it as a rare Koi Saddle Bag from Christian Dior's autumn/winter 2003 runway collection, the Daily Mail reported.The bag was identified as a limited-edition Christian Dior Koi Saddle Bag designed by John Galliano for the brand's autumn/winter 2003 runway season.£80 charity shop find identified as rare DiorThe handbag had initially been estimated at between £800 and £1,200. Its eventual sale price was more than six times the upper end of that estimate, driven by strong buyer interest.Kingham's said the bag was made in extremely limited numbers and is highly sought after by collectors of archival luxury handbags.The auction house said the owner had brought the bag in specifically to establish whether it was genuine. After specialists confirmed its identity and explained its significance, she decided to put it up for auction.Galliano design dates back to 2003The bag was created during John Galliano's time as Christian Dior's creative director. The British designer held the position from 1996 to 2011 and became known for experimental designs during his career.The Koi Saddle Bag forms part of Dior's Saddle Bag history, a line that became closely associated with Galliano's work at the fashion house.Its limited production is a major factor behind its appeal among collectors, according to Kinghams.A spokesman for the auction house said some collectors regard the particular model as a "Holy Grail" handbag because so few were produced.Bag sells for £7,870 after biddingThe final price reached £7,870 at Kinghams, turning the charity-shop purchase into a substantial return for its owner.Sophie Osborne, Kinghams' designer goods specialist, said the discovery was particularly notable because the bag had been found outside the specialist luxury market."It was the auction of the year for me," Osborne said.She added that discovering such a rare Dior and Galliano bag had been found in a charity shop was extraordinary and could prove to be the most significant find of her career.You use AI every day.
